analysis.one_liner: Makes the IRS's free online tax-filing program permanent and blocks restrictions on it.
analysis.headline: The bill to make the IRS's free Direct File program permanent, backed by 40 senators, has sat in the Senate Finance Committee with no hearing or vote since it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill writes the IRS Direct File program into law so it cannot be ended by a future administration's decision. It would let tens of millions of taxpayers prepare and file their federal returns online for free, using data the IRS already has, and would ban any agreement that stops the Treasury Department from offering its own filing service. It also moves employer and bank reporting deadlines earlier so the government can pre-fill more of your return.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, especially the tens of millions who pay commercial tax-prep companies or fee-based software each year to file a return the government already has most of the data for. The bill guarantees the service is free, requires it to work on phones and in multiple languages, and targets it to people likely to be eligible [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers who pay to file returns

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the Treasury Secretary to operate a federal, government-owned online program where taxpayers can prepare and file individual income tax returns at no cost, with no fee allowed for its use [S2].

It bars the Treasury Secretary from entering any agreement that would restrict the government's right to provide tax preparation or filing services, and voids any such existing agreements within 30 days of enactment [S2].

The program must use IRS data to simplify filing, including seamlessly importing IRS records into a return at the taxpayer's election, and must offer live customer support, mobile access, plain language, and multiple languages [S2].

For taxable years after 2027, at least half of taxpayers in participating states must be eligible, with eligibility expanded as far as possible; states without income taxes or that integrate their own filing qualify as participating states, and integrating states can get $1 million grants [S2].

It moves deadlines for employer and bank information returns earlier (generally January 31 for returns with written statements like W-2s, and March 31 for most other electronic information returns), so IRS-held data can actually be used to pre-fill returns [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The commercial tax-preparation industry, which collects filing and add-on fees from taxpayers who would otherwise use the free government program, and to a small extent taxpayers generally, through the bill's authorization of appropriations to run and promote the program through fiscal year 2035 [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes spending 'such sums as may be necessary' for fiscal years 2026 through 2035 with no cost estimate, so taxpayers ultimately fund the program, its marketing campaign, and state grants [S2].

Eligibility is initially limited: only taxpayers in states that integrate their own filing or that have no state income tax are covered, and even there the requirement is only that half of taxpayers be eligible after 2027, leaving many filers initially outside the program [S2].
The taxpayer still bears full responsibility for the accuracy of the return, so users of the free system can face the same audit exposure as users of paid software [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is direct and recurring: a free, government-run way to file that can pull data the IRS already holds, cutting out per-return fees and upsells for millions of households. The costs are real but modest by federal standards — an annual appropriations commitment and lost revenue for tax-prep companies. The main design weakness is that the initial eligibility floor (50% of taxpayers in participating states) and the state-by-state structure mean many filers would not be covered right away, though the bill directs continued expansion.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on February 26, 2026, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled since [S4].

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on February 26, 2026, joined by 40 cosponsors including Senators Wyden, Schumer, Sanders, and King, all from the Democratic caucus or allied independents [S2][S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day, and the action record shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote [S4].

The bill's core provision voiding agreements that restrict the Treasury Secretary from providing filing services is aimed at the practice of the government agreeing not to compete with commercial tax-prep software [S2].

The bill codifies Direct File in the tax code with detailed service requirements — free of fees, government-owned, IRS-data-driven, mobile-accessible, multilingual, and promoted with a mass marketing campaign — plus annual reports to Congress on usage and barriers [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the commercial tax-prep industry, which keeps the filing-fee market while the program remains outside the statute and can be ended by administrative decision.

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to codify Direct File and bar agreements restricting IRS filing services.

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill in the committee with jurisdiction over it.

for.name: Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill alongside the full Senate Democratic caucus's leadership.

for.name: Senate Democratic caucus and allied independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it the entire Democratic side of the chamber's support on day one.

against.name: Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action to schedule a hearing or markup after the bill was referred to his committee.

against.name: Commercial tax-preparation industry (Intuit, H&R Block and peers)
against.role: Paid tax-filing software and services companies
against.what_they_did: Long opposed a free government filing option and supported restrictions on the IRS offering its own service, the practice this bill would prohibit.

against.name: Trump administration
against.what_they_did: Reported plans to wind down the Direct File pilot program, which the bill would counter by writing the program into statute.

sides.party_line_note: All 41 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats or independents who caucus with Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the Republican-controlled Finance Committee has not acted on it [S3][S4].

industries.industry: Commercial tax-preparation and software companies (Intuit, H&R Block and peers)
industries.note: Their business model — charging per-return fees and selling add-ons for data the government already holds — would face a free public alternative. The bill goes further and voids any agreement in which the government promised not to compete with them [S2].
A free federal option would reduce demand for paid preparation where filers qualify, affecting seasonal preparer jobs, while eligible taxpayers save money directly [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors and the bill sitting in the Republican-chaired Finance Committee without a hearing, it is unlikely to move this session; similar codification bills typically advance only if the committee schedules a markup or a larger tax bill picks up the provision, which the record gives no sign of [S4].
